content:
A tree just came through your roof. It is dark, it is loud, and your first instinct is to panic. Do not. The next twenty four hours decide whether this becomes a manageable repair or a much bigger problem.

We have responded to storm calls in the middle of the night more times than we can count. Here is exactly what to do, in order, starting right now.

Get Everyone to Safety First

Before you touch anything, check for immediate danger. A cracked ceiling, sagging drywall, or exposed wiring means you leave that room immediately.

Do not walk under the damaged section to inspect it up close. Roofs that look stable after impact can shift hours later, and a second collapse is far more dangerous than the first one.

Watch for These Warning Signs

  • Water pooling on the ceiling or running down interior walls
  • Cracking or popping sounds from the attic or roofline
  • A visible sag in the ceiling directly below the damage
  • Any smell of gas, which means you evacuate and call emergency services immediately

If you see any of these, get everyone out and call for professional help before doing anything else.

Stop Further Damage Without Making It Worse

Once everyone is safe, your next job is to limit the damage, not fix it. That distinction matters more than most homeowners realize in the moment.

Move furniture and belongings away from the affected area if it is safe to do so. If water is actively entering the home, place buckets or tarps to catch it, but do not climb onto the roof yourself. This is not the moment for a ladder and a flashlight. Emergency roof repair is a job for a licensed crew with the right equipment and training, not a homeowner improvising in the dark.

Call a Licensed Emergency Contractor, Not Just Anyone

This is the step people get wrong most often. In a panic, homeowners call the first number that shows up in a search, and that number is not always attached to a licensed, insured company.

I always advise clients to ask two questions before letting anyone on their roof after storm damage: are you licensed and insured, and can you document the damage for my insurance claim. If the answer to either is unclear, keep calling. Our emergency services team is built for exactly this moment, with crews ready to respond around the clock.

Document Everything Before Cleanup Begins

Your insurance company will ask for proof, and proof gathered before cleanup is worth far more than a description after the fact.

  • Photograph the damage from multiple angles, inside and outside
  • Note the time and date the tree fell, as closely as you can estimate
  • Keep a written record of every call you make and every name you speak with
  • Do not throw away damaged materials until your adjuster has seen them or approved disposal

This documentation becomes the backbone of your insurance claim, and skipping it is one of the most common reasons claims get delayed or underpaid.

A Real Storm Call, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa woke up to a tree through their roof at two in the morning during a summer storm. We had a crew tarping the opening by three fifteen, less than ninety minutes after the first call.

Our team photographed the structural damage before any tarping began, which gave the homeowner's insurance adjuster everything needed to approve the claim without a second site visit. The permanent repair was scheduled within the week, and the family stayed in their home the entire time. You can see how a similar case unfolded from first call to final repair on our recent projects page.

How Insurance Claim Assistance Actually Works

Most homeowners have never filed a major property claim before, and the process feels designed to confuse. It does not have to.

I prioritize a strategy where our team documents the damage the same way an adjuster would, before the adjuster even arrives. This removes the guesswork and speeds up approval. Our insurance claim assistance service exists specifically to bridge that gap between what happened and what your policy covers, so you are not negotiating alone.

A tree falling on your roof is stressful enough without also becoming a crash course in insurance paperwork. That is not a burden you should carry by yourself.

What Happens After the Emergency Response

Once the roof is stabilized and the claim is documented, the real repair work begins. This is where a single accountable team matters more than most homeowners expect.

We have seen firsthand how splitting emergency response and permanent repair across two different companies creates gaps. Details get lost, timelines slip, and nobody takes full responsibility for the final result. One team handling stabilization through completion means one warranty, one point of contact, and one standard of work throughout.

Final Thoughts

A tree falling on your roof is frightening, but the first twenty four hours are manageable if you follow the right order: safety first, limit damage, call a licensed emergency crew, and document everything before cleanup starts. Handle those four steps correctly, and the rest of the recovery becomes a process instead of a crisis.

faqs.q: How fast can an emergency contractor respond after a tree falls on my roof?
faqs.a: Most licensed emergency crews can be on site within thirty to ninety minutes of your call, especially during active storm events.

faqs.q: Will my homeowners insurance cover a tree falling on my roof?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes, if the tree fell due to a storm or other covered event. Proper documentation at the time of the incident is essential to a smooth claim.

faqs.q: Should I try to tarp the roof myself before help arrives?
faqs.a: No. Climbing onto a storm damaged roof in the dark is dangerous. Wait for a licensed crew with the right safety equipment.

faqs.q: How long does a full roof repair take after emergency stabilization?
faqs.a: Once the roof is tarped and the claim is documented, a full repair typically takes one to three weeks depending on the extent of the damage.

faqs.q: What if the tree damaged more than just the roof?
faqs.a: A licensed contractor should assess the full structure, including attic framing and interior ceilings, not just the visible roof damage, before beginning repairs.
